tldr: AutoBio+ is a simulation benchmark for dexterous manipulation in biology laboratories. It integrates dynamic visual phenomena like flames, vapor, and bubbles with photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds, enabling parallel evaluation. Evaluating modern robot learning policies revealed that contact-rich precision tasks and language-conditioned visual grounding remain major open challenges.
hero_caption: An overview of the 14 laboratory tasks in AutoBio+ (top) and the three dynamic experimental phenomena introduced in this work (bottom: vapor, flame, and bubbles). Beyond delicate manual interactions like pipetting and opening instruments, it reproduces evolving visual conditions as laboratory procedures unfold.
overview:
Autonomous laboratories (AutoLabs), where robots run experiments on their own, have recently attracted major attention. Traditional automation relies heavily on dedicated, hardcoded machines. However, changing a biological protocol often requires extensive hardware re-engineering. Instead, researchers look forward to general-purpose robots with dexterous multi-fingered hands or grippers. Such robots could flexibly handle pipettes, tweezers, and centrifuges just like human researchers.

Yet, accurately simulating biology labs to evaluate robot learning policies is surprisingly tough. Real laboratories frequently exhibit dynamic phenomena—such as bunsen burner flames, dense vapor from liquid nitrogen, and foaming solutions. These dynamic effects heavily disrupt a robot's visual inputs. Existing benchmarks focus mostly on moving objects around in static rooms. They fail to capture these experiment-specific visual shifts and contact-rich, fine-grained manipulations.

To tackle this, the authors built AutoBio+, an evaluation platform that simulates biology lab environments and dexterous manipulation accurately and fast. It adopts a hybrid rendering pipeline: 6 real-world biology labs are reconstructed as high-fidelity backgrounds using 3D Gaussian Splatting, while foreground experimental tools are physically driven by a physics engine. In addition, a lightweight particle system models dynamic flames, vapor, and bubbles, while a Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) enables scalable demonstration collection and policy evaluation.

Evaluating modern policies—including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—across 12 tasks showed that while coarse motions like closing lids succeed, success rates plummet on tasks requiring sub-millimeter fingertip control or language-conditioned visual grounding, such as tweezer handling or precise tube insertion. Real-world experiments further confirm that simulation data rendered with photorealistic backgrounds dramatically eases the sim-to-real transfer.
contributions: Built a new benchmark tailored to biological laboratories, featuring 4 robot embodiments (dexterous hands and parallel grippers) across 14 precision manipulation tasks.
Integrated dynamic visual effects of flames, vapor, and bubbles that evolve with experiment progress using a lightweight particle system.
Developed a hybrid rendering pipeline combining real-lab 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds with physics simulation, balancing high realism with high throughput at hundreds of frames per second.
Proposed a Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and a decoupled simulation-rendering pipeline, enabling efficient, large-scale demonstration collection and parallel evaluation.

sections.heading: Why is robotic laboratory automation so difficult?
sections.summary: Automating biology laboratories requires general-purpose dexterous robots that adapt flexibly when protocols change. However, existing benchmarks center on static environments and cannot evaluate time-varying visual phenomena like flames or vapor, nor delicate manual tasks. This paper proposes AutoBio+ to simulate both accurately and fast.
sections.details:
Efforts to automate biological laboratories with robots are advancing rapidly. Yet, most conventional systems tightly couple dedicated hardware devices designed for only single tasks. Whenever a protocol, reagent, or tool changes slightly, the entire hardware setup often needs substantial re-engineering.

This is why general-purpose manipulators equipped with dexterous multi-fingered hands or grippers are in high demand. If a robot can aspirate with a pipette, pick up small specimens with tweezers, and insert tubes into racks like a human, adopting a new protocol only requires updating the software policy through imitation learning or reinforcement learning.

While many robot learning benchmarks exist for home or factory settings, biology labs pose distinct challenges. Everyday procedures involve dynamic phenomena whose visual appearance changes drastically over time—burners ignite, liquid nitrogen releases dense white vapor, and vortex mixers create bubbles. Existing simulators simply cannot evaluate a policy's robustness against these disturbances.

To bridge this gap, this work introduces AutoBio+. Supporting 14 tasks across 4 arm-and-hand embodiments, it blends dynamic effects like flames and vapor with photorealistic real-world backgrounds. This setup makes it possible to evaluate manipulation policies under remarkably true-to-life conditions.

sections.heading: Evolution and current landscape of robot learning benchmarks
sections.summary: Robot manipulation policies have progressed from Diffusion Policies and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to World Action Models (WAMs) that predict future states. Meanwhile, existing benchmarks remain biased toward two-finger grippers in household setups or static hand manipulation, leaving a void for dynamic laboratory manipulation benchmarks.
sections.details:
Visuomotor policies that generate robot actions directly from visual inputs have made tremendous progress in recent years.

- **Policy model trends**: Transformers initially emerged to output action chunks, followed by Diffusion Policies capable of capturing multimodal contact behaviors. More recently, research has expanded into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that integrate action generation into large vision-language models, as well as World Action Models (WAMs) that anticipate future visual states resulting from actions.

- **Differences from existing benchmarks**: General benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO standardize on parallel two-finger grippers, leaving them unable to assess human-like coordinated finger motions such as depressing a pipette plunger with a thumb. Conversely, multi-fingered benchmarks like Bi-DexHands and DexVerse focus purely on hand movement without covering the diverse lab tools or dynamic visual shifts seen in wet labs.

Lab-focused works like Chemistry3D and LabUtopia exist, but they still rely primarily on simple gripper grasping. Even the predecessor AutoBio simplified hand movements into basic open-close actions. AutoBio+ significantly broadens the scope, providing an all-around benchmark with richer tasks and sophisticated visual effects.

sections.heading: The simulation secrets behind physics and photorealism
sections.summary: Built on the mjlab physics engine, AutoBio+ integrates a particle system for dynamic phenomena, a hybrid rendering pipeline blending real-world 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds with MuJoCo rendering, and GPU parallelization. This achieves an approximate 70x rendering speedup over AutoBio while delivering an overwhelmingly realistic visual environment.
sections.details:
### III-A Particle system for dynamic laboratory phenomena
Simulating laboratory flames or steam strictly with computational fluid dynamics is prohibitively expensive and prevents parallel training. Instead, the authors developed a lightweight particle system inspired by game engines.

Each particle holds attributes for position, color, opacity, and size, and is updated strictly for rendering independent of the physics engine. Combining a deterministic upward buoyancy vector $\mathbf{d}_i(\mathbf{x}_i, t)$ with random perturbations $\boldsymbol{\eta}_i(t)$ that produce flickering, it depicts surprisingly realistic flames, liquid nitrogen vapor, and beaker bubbles at negligible compute cost.

### III-B Hybrid rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting
To achieve visual realism while guaranteeing exact collision and contact calculations between tools and hands, the benchmark uses a hybrid approach: real backgrounds combined with simulated hands and tools. Six real biology laboratories were scanned to reconstruct high-fidelity background models via 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS).

During rendering, foreground masks $M$ from the simulator ensure that foreground tools and robots are precisely simulated and rendered in MuJoCo, while the lab benches and surrounding rooms are composited from 3DGS. This yields visuals indistinguishable from real laboratories without compromising physical interaction accuracy.

### III-C High-throughput parallelized pipeline
All of these components are architected for batched execution on GPUs. In benchmark tests (two cameras, 640x480 resolution, 339 frames), the Blender-based rendering in AutoBio took 1,092 seconds. In contrast, this pipeline finished in just 15.57 seconds—a 70.14x speedup. It adds only an 11.6% overhead compared to raw MuJoCo rendering (13.95 seconds).

sections.heading: 14 laboratory tasks and scalable high-quality demo generation
sections.summary: The benchmark contains 14 tasks structured across four pillars: functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. Combining grasp optimization, human visual inspection, and a Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM), it automatically and efficiently collects high-quality demonstration data.
sections.details:
### IV-A Four pillars of task design
AutoBio+ tasks go far beyond pick-and-place, capturing the core difficulties of biology experiments across four categories:

- **Functional Tool Use**: Properly using tool functions, such as attaching pipette tips, aspirating liquids, or pinching specimens with tweezers.
- **Precision Manipulation**: Demanding fine multi-fingered coordination, such as inserting tubes into narrow rack slots or tightening and loosening screw caps.
- **Language-Conditioned Visual Grounding**: Interpreting language prompts like 'insert the tube into slot row 2, column 3' to locate and interact with the target in visual observations.
- **Instrument Operation**: Opening and closing centrifuges or thermal cyclers (PCR machines), and turning dials on mixer control panels.

### IV-B Automated pipeline for high-quality demonstrations
To collect demonstration data for imitation learning, the authors designed a refined generation pipeline.

First comes grasp synthesis. Using optimization methods (Dexonomy and Lightning Grasp), candidate grasps are sampled at scale. The simulator then filters out invalid poses suffering from joint limits, collisions, or slipping. Finally, human inspectors review candidates to ensure fingers do not unnaturally penetrate objects and that grasps look natural before saving them into the dataset.

Next, trajectories are generated automatically via a Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM). Each task is broken into stages like 'approach,' 'grasp,' and 'transport,' advancing asynchronously across parallel environments. Crucially, camera rendering is completely skipped during physics rollouts. Only successful trajectories are fetched from buffers and rendered in batch afterward. Skipping redundant rendering enables lightning-fast dataset generation.

captions.F3: The workflow for grasp synthesis and parallel data collection (PFSM). Optimized grasp candidates are filtered by physical constraints and checked by humans for naturalness, after which the Parallel Finite-State Machine rapidly gathers successful demonstrations.

sections.heading: Benchmarking modern AI policies and transferring to real robots
sections.summary: Four representative policies—Diffusion Policy, π0.5, GR00T-N1.7, and Fast-WAM—were benchmarked in simulation. Real-world experiments using a UR5e arm and an XHand also proved that training on simulation data with 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds substantially boosts real-world transfer performance.
sections.details:
### V-A Performance gaps uncovered in simulation
Four policy architectures were benchmarked: standard Diffusion Policy, the state-of-the-art open VLA model $\pi_{0.5}$, the humanoid dexterous foundation model GR00T-N1.7, and the predictive World Action Model Fast-WAM. Evaluated across 12 tasks over three random seeds, each policy completed 300 trials per task.

Results revealed drastic performance splits depending on task characteristics. On low-precision contact tasks like Close Centrifuge Lid, GR00T-N1.7 achieved a 100% success rate. However, on contact-rich precision tasks like using tweezers, mounting pipette tips, or capping tubes, success rates dropped sharply across every model.

### V-B Sim-to-real transfer with real robot hardware
To verify whether simulation-trained policies transfer to reality, real-world experiments were conducted using a UR5e arm and an XHand dexterous hand.

In a few-shot setting combining 10 real-world demonstrations with 90 simulation-generated demonstrations, the robot attempted tube insertion into a rack. Policies trained with standard MuJoCo backgrounds were compared against those trained with 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds. Using milestone-based scoring (up to 10 points over 20 trials), the model trained with standard backgrounds reached a normalized score of only 17%, whereas the model with photorealistic 3DGS backgrounds scored 66%. Photorealistic backgrounds substantially closed the sim-to-real gap.

sections.heading: Three key bottlenecks in current robotic AI
sections.summary: Analyzing the benchmark results points to clear shortcomings in state-of-the-art robot policies. Specifically, three core bottlenecks stand out: language-conditioned visual grounding struggles, over-relying on multi-fingered pre-training, and high failure rates in contact-rich precision tasks.
sections.details:
The findings provide valuable takeaways for future robot learning research:

- **Language-conditioned visual grounding is the biggest roadblock**: On tasks requiring spatial grounding—such as inserting a tube into a specific row and column or setting a dial to a target value—most models failed completely with 0% success rates. Even the predictive Fast-WAM showed no advantage over VLA models. This indicates that prior to predicting future states, policies fundamentally lack the vision-language capability to ground instructions into exact 3D coordinates.

- **Dexterous hand pre-training alone is not enough**: Although GR00T-N1.7 was pre-trained on large-scale dexterous hand data and performed well on coarse lid closing, it struggled on millimeter-precision fingertip tasks like pinching tweezers or twisting caps. General-purpose hand pre-training alone is insufficient; training data and controllers must account for task-specific contact dynamics.

- **High failure rates on contact-rich manipulation**: Compared to nonprehensile pushing or pulling, tasks involving rapid friction and contact transitions—tweezing, capping, and tip mounting—consistently suffered low success rates. Current vision-based policies still lack mechanisms to perceive subtle contact states and adjust fingertip forces in real time.

sections.heading: Future outlook: scaling tasks and modeling fluids
sections.summary: While AutoBio+ makes significant strides in lab manipulation, expanding tasks and 3D assets still requires manual steps. Furthermore, while the particle system is lightweight and visually appealing, it does not fully simulate fluid dynamics inside beakers, opening avenues for future methods like 4D Gaussian Splatting.
sections.details:
The authors frankly note the current limitations and exciting directions for future work:

- **Scalability of tasks and assets**: While 14 tasks are provided, they represent only a fraction of full-scale biological experiments. Grasp synthesis and state machine design still involve human checks. Future iterations could use generative AI to automatically synthesize 3D labware assets and procedural task scenarios, significantly scaling the benchmark.

- **Fidelity of fluid and dynamic phenomena**: Although the particle system balances visual realism and rendering speed well, it does not physically simulate surface tension in dripping pipette droplets or viscous fluid behaviors in beakers. To support more rigorous evaluations, adopting 4D Gaussian Splatting or dynamic neural fields to model fluid flows and container interactions with higher physical fidelity remains an exciting future direction.

sections.heading: Wrapping up: a major step toward fully automated laboratories
sections.summary: AutoBio+ is a dexterous manipulation benchmark for biology labs that incorporates dynamic phenomena and photorealistic backgrounds. It highlights the strengths and weaknesses of current policies and validates the benefit of photorealistic simulation through real-world transfer. This platform is expected to accelerate practical autonomous laboratory robots.
sections.details:
This paper introduced AutoBio+, a dexterous manipulation benchmark reproducing the realistic visual conditions and dynamic phenomena of wet biology laboratories.

By incorporating time-evolving visual elements like flames, vapor, and bubbles, and uniting 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds with MuJoCo physics in a hybrid rendering pipeline, it delivers environments visually indistinguishable from real labs alongside high-throughput parallel execution. The PFSM-driven pipeline also streamlines the scalable generation of high-quality demonstrations.

Extensive benchmarking with modern robot learning models revealed that even state-of-the-art architectures still face immense hurdles with contact-rich precision manipulation and language-conditioned spatial grounding. With AutoBio+ publicly released, it is poised to accelerate the development of more robust, dexterous laboratory robots.

takeaways: Automating biology labs requires robustness against visual disturbances from dynamic phenomena like flames and vapor; AutoBio+ establishes a standardized benchmark to evaluate this.

Hybrid rendering combining real 3D Gaussian Splatting backgrounds with simulated foregrounds drastically narrows the sim-to-real gap without sacrificing rendering speed (real-robot success score improved from 17% to 66%).
Even leading VLA and WAM architectures struggle heavily on tasks requiring visual grounding of language-specified slots or dials to guide precision manipulation.

Large-scale multi-fingered pre-training alone is not a silver bullet; contact-rich precision tasks like pinching tweezers or twisting caps still demand task-specific fine-grained fingertip control data.
limitations: While the particle system produces fast and convincing visual effects, it does not simulate fluid mechanics such as surface tension or liquid viscosity.
Building the 14 tasks and validating grasp poses still involves human visual inspection, meaning the benchmark cannot yet procedurally generate endless assets and tasks completely autonomously.
Real-world robot validation was restricted to a few-shot tube insertion task, rather than testing all 14 benchmark tasks on hardware.
